column11: Why does FNH retain hepatobiliary contrast while its central scar does not?
column12: FNH contains functioning hepatocytes and biliary ductules, so the lesion can take up and retain hepatobiliary contrast. The central scar is composed of biliary ductules and venules but behaves differently from the surrounding hepatocellular tissue and does not retain gadoxetate. Core also emphasizes that this central region is not a true fibrotic scar and may enhance late with extracellular contrast. Imaging pivot: lesion-level hepatobiliary retention with scar nonretention supports FNH over adenoma.

column11: Why does a cavernous hemangioma show peripheral nodular enhancement with progressive centripetal fill-in?

Contrast first enters the peripheral vascular lakes, producing discontinuous nodular blood-pool enhancement, then progressively fills more central vascular spaces on later phases. Imaging pivot: enhancement should match the blood pool through phases, which separates hemangioma from most solid hypervascular tumors.

column11: How does the regenerative-nodule to dysplastic-nodule to HCC pathway explain arterialization of HCC?

Regenerative and most dysplastic nodules remain predominantly portal-venous supplied, whereas malignant progression is accompanied by increasing neovascularity. The result is arterial-phase hyperenhancement of HCC relative to background liver, with classic lesions later becoming relatively hypoenhancing (washout). Imaging pivot: increasing arterialization is a core discriminator along the hepatocarcinogenesis pathway.

column11: Why can hepatobiliary imaging and chemical-shift MRI help separate hepatic adenoma from FNH?

The absent bile-duct component explains the usual lack/paucity of HIDA uptake and helps distinguish adenoma from FNH, which contains biliary ductules. Some adenomas also contain intracellular lipid, producing signal loss on out-of-phase chemical-shift MRI. Imaging pivot: hepatobiliary/biliary-duct behavior and intracellular lipid provide composition-based separation from FNH.

column11: Why does mass-forming cholangiocarcinoma show progressive delayed enhancement?
column12: The source attributes the progressive arterial-to-portal-to-delayed enhancement pattern to abundant fibrotic stroma. Fibrous tissue accumulates and retains contrast later than the more cellular portions of the mass, producing progressive delayed enhancement. Imaging pivot: progressive fibrotic enhancement plus capsular retraction and biliary obstruction favors cholangiocarcinoma over hypervascular hepatocellular lesions.

column6: Large regenerative nodules in Budd-Chiari syndrome
column11: What explains hepatobiliary-agent retention in large regenerative nodules associated with Budd-Chiari syndrome?
column12: The fused source states that persistent gadobenate uptake/retention within these nodules indicates functional hepatocytes with deficient biliary ducts. Thus, despite hypervascularity and central scars, retained hepatobiliary agent supports regenerative hepatocellular tissue rather than nonhepatocellular metastasis. Imaging pivot: functional hepatocyte retention is a composition clue within the Budd-Chiari regenerative-nodule pattern.

column13: What is the key board pitfall when a scar-containing FNH is compared with a close malignant mimic, and what safety check prevents the error?
column14:
Trap: Treating any central scar in a hypervascular liver mass as diagnostic of FNH.
Safety check: Interrogate scar T2 signal, calcification, delayed enhancement, hepatobiliary-agent behavior, and aggressiveness.
Discriminator: FNH favors homogeneous arterial enhancement, a T2-bright scar with late extracellular enhancement, and lesion-level hepatobiliary retention; fibrolamellar HCC favors a fibrotic T1/T2-low scar, frequent scar calcification in the fused article, and may show nodal/vascular/biliary spread.
Why it happens: Both can be large hypervascular masses with central scars.

column13: What prevents a giant hemangioma with a central scar from being mistaken for a scarred malignant liver mass?
column14:
Trap: Focusing on the central scar/calcification and ignoring the enhancement kinetics.
Safety check: Compare enhancement with blood pool on every phase.
Discriminator: Peripheral discontinuous nodular enhancement that matches vessels and progressively fills centripetally is the defining hemangioma clue; very high T2 signal further supports it.
Why it happens: Giant hemangiomas can have nonenhancing central degeneration/fibrosis and even calcification, mimicking a necrotic or scarred tumor.

column13: What is the central-scar pitfall in hepatic adenoma, and what check prevents overcalling a true scar?
column14:
Trap: Calling a central nonenhancing/low-density region a true scar.
Safety check: Look for source-supported components such as hemorrhage, necrosis, fibrosis, or intracellular fat and assess hepatobiliary contrast behavior.
Discriminator: Adenoma may show hemorrhage/necrosis/fat/fibrosis and chemical-shift signal loss; FNH more characteristically retains hepatobiliary contrast and has a characteristic scar behavior.
Why it happens: Central heterogeneous components in adenoma can visually mimic a scar.

column13: What prevents a fibrotic cholangiocarcinoma from being mistaken for another scar-containing liver mass?

column6: Large regenerative nodules in Budd-Chiari syndrome
column13: What is the board pitfall when multiple hypervascular scar-containing nodules are seen in Budd-Chiari syndrome?
column14:
Trap: Assuming multiplicity plus arterial hypervascularity automatically means metastases or multifocal HCC.
Safety check: Integrate chronic Budd-Chiari morphology and hepatobiliary-agent behavior.
Discriminator: Multiple regenerative nodules can be hypervascular, contain central scars, and retain hepatobiliary agent because they contain functional hepatocytes; nonliver-primary metastases do not show this hepatocyte uptake.
Why it happens: Hypervascular regenerative nodules can closely mimic neoplasm on arterial-phase imaging.

Sulfur colloid can demonstrate Kupffer cells (about 1/3 of the time).

column15: For hepatic cavernous hemangioma, what CT/MRI pattern is expected?

Peripheral discontinuous nodular enhancement matching blood pool.
Progressive centripetal fill-in on later phases.

Circumscribed, usually homogeneously echogenic mass.

column15: For conventional HCC, what CT/MRI appearance and invasive behavior are source-supported?
column16:
Arterial-phase hyperenhancement with portal/delayed washout and enhancing capsule when classic.
MRI: slightly T2 hyperintense; may restrict diffusion.
Large lesions may show mosaic architecture, necrosis, fat, or blood products.
Often invades portal/hepatic veins, IVC, or bile ducts.

column15: For hepatic adenoma, what imaging features help distinguish it from FNH?
column16:
Arterial hyperenhancement with iso-/hypointensity to liver on portal/delayed phases.
May be heterogeneous from fat or hemorrhage; intracellular lipid can drop signal out of phase.
No specific US appearance.
Usually photopenic on sulfur colloid and shows little/no HIDA uptake because bile ducts are absent.
Exam pivot: Fat/hemorrhage plus absent biliary-duct behavior favors adenoma.
